title: Indexing 206M+ Podcast Subtitle Lines and Pairing Them with PubMed & Wikipedia Citations
summary:
When I research a topic through long-form podcasts or university lectures (say, sleep architecture, creatine for cognition, or semiconductor supply chains), I keep hitting two annoying walls:

  1. Searching YouTube drops you into three-hour episodes full of sponsor reads and detours.
  2. Dropping a link into an LLM summarizer strips away the speaker's actual tone, caveats, and source provenance.

Over the past few weeks I built PastNoise to scratch that exact itch. Instead of generating another text summary, it searches across 206M+ timestamped spoken subtitle lines and stitches 5 to 6 non-duplicate primary speakers into a single continuous screening room, paired with side-by-side Wikipedia, PubMed, Crossref, and OpenAlex citations.

Three Small Engineering Choices That Made the Biggest Difference

1. Filtering sponsor reads before picking clips (not after)
Early builds looked fine until a flagship topic pulled two Hostinger and Tonal ad reads from top podcasts. Moving a strict sponsor/outro detector ahead of act selection and hydrating 16 candidate windows first (then backfilling clean distinct channels) dropped sponsor contamination to zero across all 58 indexed screenings.

2. Rendering full bilingual transcripts in SSR DOM with #act-X-t-Y citation anchors
Single-page tabs that unmount transcript DOM hide 95% of spoken text from search engines and make it impossible to quote a speaker accurately. Keeping every chapter's timestamped transcript inside lightweight

accordions with click-to-copy citation links lets readers jump straight to the exact second and verify the primary quote.

3. Preserving original subtitle sequence IDs (origSeq) when splitting long cues
Auto-captions often pack 220+ characters into one cue. Splitting cues down to readable 96-character lines broke pre-translated subtitle lookups whenever the original sequence index passed 100. Keeping an explicit origSeq field alongside sequential display IDs solved alignment cleanly for English, Simplified Chinese, and Traditional Chinese (via OpenCC at zero extra LLM cost).

Open Assets You Can Reuse (CC BY 4.0)

If you prefer local notes or want clean benchmark data for citation-grounded RAG experiments, I exported the entire 58-topic curated archive under CC BY 4.0:

  • Obsidian Knowledge Vault (58 dossiers + 25 Thinker MOCs): github.com/nonacosa/pastnoise-obsidian-vault
  • Hugging Face Dataset (491 ad-filtered clips with YouTube timestamps + DOIs): huggingface.co/datasets/pkwenda/pastnoise-primary-citations
  • Free Hydration Utility: Galpin Equation Hydration Calculator
  • Full Interactive Screening Room (free without login): pastnoise.com

Curious how other builders here handle long-form audio/video retrieval and hallucination checks without losing the original speaker's voice.

title: npm stopped taking weekends
summary:
For six years, npm had the same week. Five busy days, then a Saturday and Sunday at about a quarter of the pace, because the people running npm install were at work and then they weren't.

Then in spring 2025 that started to go. npm's downloads API has a daily total for the whole registry going back to 2015, so here's a weekend day as a share of a weekday, quarter by quarter, with PyPI beside it:

A weekend day's downloads as a share of a weekday's, npm and PyPI (the data)

The median weekend day over the median weekday, each quarter. npm's from its downloads API, PyPI's
from ClickHouse's public ClickPy data. Days npm reports as zero
and the Christmas fortnight are left out, and 2026 Q4 runs to 19 November.

npm sat between 23% and 29% for 25 quarters in a row. It's at 47% now.

I was pulling those totals to see how big the AI boom looks from the registry's side, and the size is daft enough on its own. npm served 292 billion downloads in October 2024, 424 billion in October 2025 and just over a trillion this October.

But a bigger registry with the same weekly shape would just be more of the same. The extra downloads since summer 2024 run at 54% on weekends, so whatever's adding them barely keeps office hours. That's close to PyPI, which has been up there as far back as the data goes.

It isn't just the new stuff

The obvious answer is all the new apps AI tools are spinning up, installing whatever's in fashion. So I looked at packages nobody starts a project with any more.

node-sass has been deprecated on npm since 2024, with a notice telling you to use sass instead. In summer 2024 it got about 286,000 downloads on a normal weekday and 62,000 on a weekend day. Now it's 155,000 and 82,000. Fewer people install it on a Tuesday than two years ago, and more do on a Saturday. TSLint, which told everyone to move to ESLint back in 2019, has nearly doubled at weekends with its weekdays flat. And left-pad, of all things, went from 21% to 59%.

Weekend downloads as a share of weekday ones, then and now (the data)

Summer 2024 is July to September, autumn 2026 is 1 October to 19 November. Medians, like the chart
above.

Packages people still use moved just as much. When I checked 507 of the biggest on 14 November, 506 had gone up by at least 10 points, and none was still under 30%. Taking the biggest few hundred out of the registry's total leaves the line where it was, so it isn't a few giants dragging the average along.

vaul is my favourite. It's a drawer component for React, and its README opens with "This repo is unmaintained". The last release was December 2024. In summer 2024 it got 76,000 downloads a weekday, and now it gets 5.4 million, because the Radix version of shadcn/ui's drawer is built on it, and AI app builders like Lovable start you off with the whole shadcn set. Lovable also puts its own Vite plugin, lovable-tagger, in the projects it makes, and of the 76,416 package.json files on GitHub that list it, 75,904 list vaul too.

Linux went first

So who's installing node-sass on a Saturday? A download count doesn't say who asked for it, but packages with a separate binary for each platform give a hint. esbuild ships one for Linux, one for Macs, one for Windows and a pile of others, and npm only fetches the one for the machine it's running on.

Linux stopped taking weekends before Macs and Windows did (the data)

Weekend downloads as a share of weekday ones for @esbuild/linux-x64, @esbuild/darwin-arm64 and
@esbuild/win32-x64, worked out the same way as the first chart.

Linux started drifting in spring 2025, while the Mac and Windows binaries didn't budge all year. They only got going in 2026, and they're at 44% and 45% now to Linux's 54%. Rollup's binaries do exactly the same. Linux is also where the volume is: 59 million esbuild installs a weekday, up from 5 million in summer 2024, against 3.5 million for Macs.

That gap rules out one boring answer. Anything that grabs packages wholesale, like a mirror or a security scanner, would fetch all three alike, and the three lines would have moved together. They didn't.

Most CI runners, containers and cloud sandboxes are Linux, so the first wave looks like machines. OpenAI's Codex cloud agent and Claude Code's general release both came out in May 2025, which lines up nicely and proves nothing. I can't read the Macs and Windows PCs. That could be people building things at weekends now that something else does the typing, or more CI on Macs, or both, and download counts can't tell them apart.

The weirdest one I found is create-vite, the thing you run to start a new Vite project. Scaffolders were always weekend-heavy, because starting a side project is a Saturday thing, and create-vite ran at 67% in summer 2024. It's at 93% now, on 12 times the volume. Vite projects get started on a Sunday nearly as often as on a Tuesday.

Checking a package yourself

This gets a package's last month from the same API and gives you its weekend average as a percentage of its weekday one:

curl -s https://api.npmjs.org/downloads/range/last-month/react | jq '
  [.downloads[] | select(.downloads > 0) | {
    n: .downloads,
    weekend: (.day | strptime("%Y-%m-%d") | mktime | strftime("%a") | test("Sat|Sun"))
  }]
  | group_by(.weekend) | map(map(.n) | add / length)
  | .[1] / .[0] * 100 | round'

It's a straight average over the last 30 days rather than the medians in the charts, so it won't match them exactly. react comes out at 57 today, and node-sass at 46. In the summer of 2024, almost everything came out somewhere around 25.

vaul's README still says it's unmaintained. Last Sunday it was downloaded 3.3 million times.

title: My Codex 5-Hour Limit Hit 0%. ChatGPT Chat Still Created the File (Sora Commander v0.5.0)
summary:
Recently my Codex 5-hour limit showed 0% left. I still had work to finish, so I opened an ordinary ChatGPT chat and asked it to create a file on my Windows PC through Sora Commander, my open-source MCP server. A small approval window popped up on my desktop. I read it, clicked Approve, and the file appeared in Explorer.

Here is that run, 26 seconds, recorded on my PC on 2026-11-21 (captions are in Japanese):

An honest caveat first: this shows that this request still ran. It does not show that tool calls never count toward any limit. ChatGPT's own message limits still apply, and plan terms can change at any time. What it does show is that the reading, running and checking happen in the ChatGPT chat I already use, so that work isn't spent from a separate coding agent's limit.

That run was on the build I've just released: v0.5.0.

What Sora Commander is (30-second version)

If you missed the first post: Sora Commander is a free, open-source (AGPL-3.0) MCP server for Windows. It connects to ChatGPT through OpenAI's Secure MCP Tunnel. ChatGPT can read and search files in folders I allow, run commands and report their output, and create or edit supported text files. Commands that aren't plainly safe, and every file create or edit, open an approval window on my PC and run only if I approve them there. There is no remote approval.

What's new in v0.5.0

This release is mostly about getting started and staying up to date with less friction.

Setup, key and update helpers

  • tools\setup.cmd creates .venv, installs the packages, copies the example tunnel settings if they're missing, runs the doctor check and lists what's left to do by hand. --check only reports.
  • tools\set-tunnel-key.cmd stores the tunnel key with hidden input, in a file only your Windows user can open. --check checks its form without showing it.
  • tools\update.cmd previews incoming releases with --check, then fast-forwards a clean main.
  • tools\install-broker-autostart.cmd (optional) starts Broker mode and then the tunnel when you sign in to Windows.

No PowerShell needed

The launchers and helpers now use only .cmd files and Python. They keep working if Windows PowerShell 5.1 becomes optional, and PowerShell 7 isn't required either. The prerequisites are now Windows 11, Python 3.13 and Git for Windows in C:\Program Files\Git.

Shorter tool help, same tools

Shared approval rules moved into the server instructions, so each tool description is shorter. Tool names and inputs are unchanged.

  • With the included launchers, ChatGPT sees 54 tools.
  • The optional read-only Muse bridge lists 36 tools, or 37 with --inbox. The six command and wait tools it could never run are gone from its list. (I wrote about the bridge in this post. It's read-only: commands are refused and no approval window opens from it. Muse is a Meta product; this project is not affiliated with or endorsed by Meta.)

Fixes I'm happy about

  • Git tools now show Japanese and other non-ASCII file names as they are, instead of \343\203... escapes. As a Japanese developer, this one was personal.
  • bridge_digest and tool_catalog report 0.5.0 instead of UNKNOWN.
  • A key check error keeps the launcher window open so you can actually read it.
  • Owner ACL errors are now a single [HOLD] line naming the file and the reason.

Quick start

Before anything else, check your ChatGPT plan. Custom MCP connections are web-only, and OpenAI's help page lists full MCP for Business and Enterprise/Edu. I use it on Plus with developer mode, including approved commands, as of November 2026, but Plus isn't listed there and that can change.

Then, roughly (the full steps are in docs/INSTALL.md):

git clone https://github.com/kurojack-jp/SoraCommander.git C:\SoraCommander
cd C:\SoraCommander
tools\setup.cmd
  1. Download tunnel-client from OpenAI's Secure MCP Tunnels guide (it isn't bundled) and put it in tools\tunnel-client\\.
  2. Create a tunnel in the OpenAI platform settings, then run tools\set-tunnel-key.cmd to store its key.
  3. Fill in the three values in %USERPROFILE%\.config\tunnel-client\sora-next.yaml, and list the folders you want to allow.
  4. Double-click tools\start-broker-mode.cmd and keep both windows open.
  5. Connect ChatGPT as OpenAI's help page describes, then in a new chat ask for ping, status and tool_catalog. tool_catalog should report 54 tools and version 0.5.0.

Updating from v0.4.0: v0.4.0 has no update helper, so update once by hand: stop the tunnel, the Broker and the Muse bridge, then in a clean checkout on main run git pull --ff-only and tools\setup.cmd --check. From then on, tools\update.cmd does it. Afterwards, restart everything and refresh the tools in ChatGPT.

Safety: what the approval window does and doesn't do

I'd rather be precise here than reassuring:

  • Commands that aren't plainly safe, and file edits, need a click at the PC. If the window can't open, the session is locked, or records can't be written, it fails closed. That also means you have to be at the PC to approve.
  • Reads need no window. ChatGPT can read your allowed folders while you're signed in, including when Broker mode is started at logon.
  • An approved command runs with your own Windows rights and can do anything your account can. The window and folder limits reduce risk; they are not a sandbox. Read each window before you click.
  • In Broker mode, a command whose outcome is unknown isn't repeated, even after a restart, until you clear it by hand.
  • It's a developer preview. status reports remote_ready: false and LOCAL_DEMO_ONLY, the code isn't signed, and there's no installer. v0.5.0 was checked on my own setup and in a fresh Windows Sandbox (where setup.cmd and the launch checks passed from an ASCII and a Japanese checkout path, without starting a tunnel). That isn't production acceptance, and there's no warranty.

Try it

  • GitHub: https://github.com/kurojack-jp/SoraCommander
  • v0.5.0 release notes (with a SHA256 for the zip): https://github.com/kurojack-jp/SoraCommander/releases/tag/v0.5.0

Issues are welcome. For security problems, please follow SECURITY.md instead of opening a public issue.

The repo and its install docs are free. If you'd rather follow a step-by-step path with screenshots and the common errors explained, there's also a paid companion guide: Sora Commander — The Complete Beginner's Guide (Gumroad).

Sora Commander is an independent project, not made, endorsed or supported by OpenAI.

Sora Commander started as "please stop making me copy-paste between the chat and my terminal." v0.5.0 doesn't change the limits; it just makes the setup shorter, so there's less standing between you and the chat you already have open.

title: How to Test Agent Memory After a Project Rename
summary:
When choosing a tool for long-term agent memory, include a project rename in your trial. title: Trap Streets for Code: How Mapmakers Caught Copiers, and How I Do It in Git
summary:
In the 1920s, two mapmakers at General Drafting, Otto G. Lindberg and Ernest Alpers, put a town on their map of New York that didn't exist. They called it Agloe, an anagram of their initials, and placed it at a dirt-road crossing in the Catskills. The idea was simple: if Agloe ever showed up on someone else's map, that someone had copied theirs.

It did. Agloe turned up on a Rand McNally map. When General Drafting objected, Rand McNally had an answer ready: Delaware County had a business on record named Agloe. Someone had read the fake town off a map and named a lodge after it. The trap worked so well that it briefly became real. The USGS still lists it today as "Agloe (Not Official)."

Mapmakers call these trap streets. Dictionaries have them too. The 1975 New Columbia Encyclopedia had a lovingly detailed entry for Lillian Virginia Mountweazel, a fountain designer and photographer of rural mailboxes, who died in an explosion while on assignment for Combustibles magazine. She never existed. In 2001, the New Oxford American Dictionary defined "esquivalience" as "the wilful avoidance of one's official responsibilities." That word never existed either, until it did.

My favorite version doesn't involve fake towns at all. In 2001 the UK's Automobile Association paid Ordnance Survey £20 million to settle a case over copied maps. Ordnance Survey said it hadn't planted deliberate mistakes. It identified the copies by their fingerprints, details like the width of the roads.

So there are three kinds of evidence: a thing you planted on purpose, a thing that behaves in a way only you'd predict, and the shape of the work itself.

That's TrapR. It's open source, it's Python with no required dependencies, and it plants all three kinds in your code.

👉 GitHub: github.com/jaykrishna316/TrapR

Why I built it

I work across several repos: Neo (multi-agent coordination), Braxis (keeps AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md in sync with the code), and a growing pile of side projects. They sprawl, and I wanted a way to actually see my own work across them: which files are mine, how the set grows over time, and whether any of it has wandered off somewhere it shouldn't be.

Git history doesn't answer that last part. It proves what you committed. It says nothing about a repo you've never seen that contains your code with your name filed off. A LICENSE file is one rm away from not existing.

I wanted a trap street.

Layer 1: the marker (my Agloe)

Every source file gets a header line like this one, which is actually sitting in TrapR's own trapr.py right now:

`

`python
python

!/usr/bin/env python3

build-id: 8113f5bb-6572d2d8`

`

It looks like boring build metadata, and that's the point. It's an HMAC:

tag = HMAC-SHA256(secret_key, file_path)[:8]

The first half is the project tag, and the second half is derived from the secret key and that file's path. Without the key, you can't forge a valid marker, and you can't tell which file a marker was made for. title: Sticky Kakeya sets over F3 grow more slowly than 2^n
summary:
This work was carried out with AI agents working in MV2's name. No human mathematician has checked it yet.

In an earlier post we wrote about a 30-point sticky Kakeya set in four dimensions over the three-element field F3, one point below the classical construction. That was a constant-factor saving. This post is about the exponential version: sticky Kakeya sets in F3^n need only about 1.98734^n points, not 2^n.

The short version

A Kakeya set in F3^n contains a full line {x, x + v, x + 2v} in every direction v. In our "sticky" family, the lines come from a map P whose j-th output coordinate depends only on the first j coordinates of the direction, a finite-field analogue of the sticky case that Wang and Zahl settled for real 3-space. The growth rate of the smallest sticky sets is controlled by one number per tree of height k: the product of its three slice sizes. The classical tree has product exactly 8^k, and the base drops below 2 as soon as some tree does better.

Nothing does better at heights 3 or 4 (exhaustive computations). At height 5 we found a tree whose three slices have 31 points each, product 31^3 = 29,791 < 8^5 = 32,768. That gives the base 31^(1/5) = 1.98734.

How the tree is built

  • Tree A, P(d) = (d1^2, -d1 d2, 0), has slices of 4, 12 and 12 points, and its last two slices are the same set.
  • Tree B, from an earlier note, has slices of 7, 7 and 13 points.
  • A's 12-point slice fits inside B's 13-point slice. Under the root map x^2, the trees A, B and a mirrored B make a height-4 tree H with slices 11, 20, 20, whose last two slices coincide.
  • A "cyclic triangle" lifts H one level, giving three slices of |H_0| + |H_1 ∪ H_2| = 11 + 20 = 31 points.

We found it by hand, from a case analysis of where a beat could hide, not by search. The test suite rebuilds every map and checks the resulting 6-dimensional set contains a line in every direction.

Is 31 the best at height 5?

Yes. A pre-registered exhaustive computation, filed before the tree was found, bounds the height-5 minimum from below. It came out at exactly 29,791. So the sticky growth base now lies between 1.90499 and 1.98734. Any further improvement needs height 6 or more, and an exact solver run for that is queued.

What it is not

This is not a new record for general Kakeya sets over F3. Constructions with base about 1.8899 have been known since 2010 (Kopparty, Lev, Saraf and Sudan), and sticky sets provably cannot reach them. The point is narrower: inside the sticky family, the classical construction is not optimal.

  • Write-up: https://www.munimtech.com/research/sticky-kakeya-sets-over-f3-beat-base-two
  • Code, data and notes (Apache-2.0, text CC BY 4.0): https://github.com/munimtechnologies/kakeya-small-fields

Questions and corrections are welcome.

title: Browser Use in DSH Agent Enhancer: Click, Debug, and Replay Saved Flows
summary:
dsh-agent-enhancer is a desktop plugin for DSH. Its Browser Use layer gives your agent a dedicated browser. It can click, type, and submit. Login state stays in its own profile, so your everyday browser is left alone.

You do not need scripting or API knowledge. Do the task once in the dedicated window, and the agent can follow the same steps. Save the recording as a flow, rerun it by name, and hand it to a scheduled task without approving every action.

The practical rule: if you click through the same web admin every day or every week, it is worth handing over. Here are scenarios that work right after install:

Role Repetitive work How it helps
E-commerce ops Export yesterday's orders, refunds, and inventory at 8:00 every day Three saved flows plus the built-in scheduler, running unattended
Finance / reconciliation Export admin data and statements on the 1st of each month, then reconcile three tables Automated except for the password step; if it gets stuck, it leaves a record
Recruiting / HR Go through new resumes and filter by keywords every Monday Read-only tabs: it can read, but cannot change anything
Marketing / competitive research Check competitor pricing and campaign pages every morning Extract plus screenshots, with changes written straight into the chat
Dev / QA Re-click the same reproduction steps in the admin UI Record once, rerun by name during regression; fix once after a redesign
Handover / onboarding Explain "where to click first" again and again A teammate demos once; the steps become a flow anyone can run next month

Three patterns cover most of these:

  • Turn repetitive work into one sentence. Record once, save, run on schedule, and check the result in the morning.
  • Read-only pages that must not change. Order details, reports, production dashboards: it can read and scroll, but clicks do nothing.
  • Keep the "how" around. A teammate demos once, the steps become a flow; when the site changes, it finishes the job and you click Remember once.

Under the hood, the actions come from a set of browser_* tools: browser_navigate opens a page, browser_snapshot reads it, browser_click / browser_type operate it, browser_scroll / browser_wait / browser_extract handle long pages, browser_list_tabs / browser_follow_tab switch tabs, browser_network / browser_console / browser_emulate debug it, browser_demonstrate records a demo, and browser_demo_recipes manages saved flows. When you need to take over and log in yourself, use browser_ask_user; there are also browser_screenshot and browser_status.

This post starts with what it can do, then walks through six areas: operation, troubleshooting, demo recording, saved flows, scheduled tasks, and boundaries. Each section ends with a concrete use case.

Operation: multiple tabs, read-only tabs, idle cleanup

Say "open the browser" in the chat, or Alt-click (Option-click on Mac) a link in the conversation, and the dedicated window starts. It has its own profile, so you log in once and stay logged in. On Mac it uses Chrome or Safari; on Windows, Chrome or Edge. It is completely separate from your daily browser. On Mac, selecting Safari drives the WebKit engine, not the Safari app you use every day.

Multiple tabs. The sidebar lists every tab; click one to switch. When navigating, you can choose to open a new tab. If a task needs to compare orders, inventory, and shipping, you do not have to cram everything into one page.

Read-only tabs. One click in the sidebar makes a tab read-only: the agent can look, but it cannot click, type, or navigate within that tab. Opening a new tab and scrolling still work. Check-only pages — reports, order details — are the safest place to use it. Even a saved flow replay is blocked by this restriction.

Idle cleanup. Idle tabs can close automatically after 10, 30, or 60 minutes, or never. The tab you are currently viewing, session-bound tabs, and the last remaining tab are never closed. The dedicated window does not pile up.

Use it for: reconciling orders across three admin pages. Open orders, inventory, and shipping in separate tabs; make inventory read-only so nobody accidentally clicks "Adjust stock"; come back from lunch and idle tabs are gone, but the login is still there.

Troubleshooting: debug tools and page emulation

When the Export button does nothing, guessing is the worst approach. Turn on Debug & Page Emulation in settings (off by default):

  • Network: method, URL, status code, duration, failure reason;
  • Console: output, uncaught exceptions, source location;
  • Page emulation: dark mode, reduced motion, viewport size.

It reads only what it needs: no request headers, cookies, or response bodies. Tokens and codes in URLs, plus links in the console, are redacted.

Startup failures do not require digging through logs either. The status bar and sidebar show the reason and the next step: feature not enabled, browser not started, WebKit missing, no usable browser on the machine, profile directory locked, and so on.

Use it for: a dead Export button. Check whether the network call returns 500 or times out, then look for console errors. Switch to a narrow viewport to rule out an overlay covering the button. Once you know the cause, change the agent's action instead of trying blindly.

Demo recording: do it once, it remembers

Some admin tasks are easier to show than to describe. Turn on Demo Recording in settings (off by default), click "Start demo" in the sidebar, and use the dedicated window normally. When you are done, click "End and view steps".

It records clicks, typing, Enter presses, and page navigations. It can record across tabs, and other tabs opened during the demo are captured. When finished, you can copy the steps or click "Send to agent" to insert them into the input box (the current conversation needs at least one message first, otherwise it asks you to send one). You can also say "let me show you" in the chat, and the agent can start a recording itself.

Password, CAPTCHA, token, and card-number fields are stored as *** only. It does not take screenshots or record network requests.

Use it for: handing over monthly reconciliation. Ask a teammate to demo it once: open the reconciliation page, pick the month, export, download, and check the three tables. Send the steps to the agent, and next month nobody has to ask "where do I click first?"

Saved flows: from a one-off demo to a reusable run

After recording, click "Save as flow" and give it a name, such as "Weekly report export". There are three ways to run it:

  • Click Run under "Saved flows" in the sidebar;
  • Say Run "Weekly report export" in the chat. The agent finds it by name and asks for approval once per run by default; Full Access or unattended mode stops the repeated prompts;
  • Hand it to the built-in Automation Tasks with unattended mode, and it runs on schedule. The next section explains how to wire that up.

It works across sessions and restarts. If the current page is not the page where recording started, it returns there first. Data stays local and only redacted steps are stored; password fields remain ***.

The sidebar row keeps only Run and "⋯"; rename and delete live in the menu, and delete asks for confirmation. Expanding the row shows editable values, run mode, and steps. Replay supports dropdowns and checkboxes. If several controls share a name and cannot be distinguished, it stops and lists the candidates instead of clicking the first one by name.

Parameters: plain language, not variable names

After saving, values worth changing — dates, email addresses, search terms — are detected automatically. Parameter names come straight from the page labels ("Start date"), so you do not have to invent variable names.

Date fields get a date picker. You can also say "last week", "this month", or "last quarter", and the agent converts it to a real date. When a value is missing, it asks in plain language: "Which start date should I use this time?"

Each value's default and display name can be changed; it can be set to "Ask me each time" or switched back to a fixed value. Every change goes into version history, and the last change can be undone.

Repair: when the site changes, it finishes the job

If the site renames a control or inserts an extra dialog, the flow gets stuck. The agent finishes the task, then offers a suggestion:

"The control in step 4 changed; it is now called 'Start date'. Remember this for next time?"

  • Remember: write the repair back into the flow and use it next time;
  • Just this once: leave the flow as it was.

Repair changes only how the control is located. It does not change values or step order. Password fields do not participate, and are never stored in the flow. Every write-back creates a version that can be undone.

Run results: what happened last time

Each saved flow records its last run: time, success / stopped at step N / failure. If it did not finish, the row shows a "Last run incomplete" badge. It stores counts and the reason it stopped, not page content.

Use it for: a weekly report export. Record once, save "Weekly report export", set "Start date" to Ask me each time, say Run "Weekly report export" with last week's start date on Monday morning, and check the run result. title: Running a video-by-code agent on one RTX 4090: the context budget is the real limit
summary:
Run an open model as a long agent (a model that calls tools in a loop on its own) on one card and the weights are rarely what stops you. The budget around them is: how much the agent can keep in view, and how long one answer may be.

We learned that with SenseNova 6.8 Code2Video, SenseTime's open 27B model that makes video by writing code. We drove it with Claude Code on one 24 GB RTX 4090 on our cloud. Ten minutes in, it had a full 12-second clip. Forty minutes in, it had no finished film. The logs and frames are in the full research write-up on running Code2Video on one RTX 4090. Here I focus on the settings.

Your settings are not the authors' settings

The SenseNova team publishes a Claude Code skill called code-video and six complete production runs. They serve the full-size model across four GPUs. Their context window (the text the model can see at once, counted in tokens, which are word pieces) is 512K tokens, and one answer may run to 64K. Their films needed between 261 and 876 turns each.

We used bartowski's 4-bit GGUF, a compressed copy of the weights (17.2 GB) for the llama.cpp server, plus a 0.93 GB vision part so the model can see images. Three Claude Code variables encode the gap:

CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS=98304   # authors: 524288
CLAUDE_AUTOCOMPACT_PCT_OVERRIDE=80     # same as the authors
CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS=16384    # authors: 64000

Without the first one, Claude Code assumes 200K for a model it does not recognize.

The trap: compaction needs room to write

Compaction is how Claude Code survives a full context. Once the window passes 80%, it has the model write a recap, throws the old history away and continues from the recap alone. The recap is a normal reply, so the output cap applies to it too.

Our 98,304-token window was full after about 19 minutes. Three recap requests followed. All three ran into the 16,384-token ceiling, none produced a usable summary, and together they ate 21 minutes until our 40-minute limit killed the run with no final film.

Compaction can work: four of the authors' six runs cleared contexts of 167K to 492K tokens, under a 64K cap. On our side two settings are under suspicion. One is the 16,384-token cap. The other is hidden reasoning, the thinking the model writes before its visible answer, which we left on and which draws from the same cap. The logs cannot tell them apart, though in a separate single request the same 4-bit file burned all 8,192 output tokens thinking and wrote no page. A bigger window, a bigger cap or reasoning off might fix it; we tried none of them.

So when you size a single-card agent, measure two things before you trust it: when the context will hit the compaction threshold, and whether one summary fits under your output cap with reasoning on.

The file check passed a wrong picture

Self-review did its job. The model opened 21 of its own stills as images, spotted two bugs and fixed both. All on-screen text matched the brief word for word.

The one fact that mattered was still wrong. The brief asked for 30 dots in a 5 by 6 rectangle. We located each dot centre in the 7.2-second frame with numpy and scipy and got 5 rows of 7 columns, one cell empty per row. The skill's file check still said yes. It only looks at resolution, frame rate and duration, never at what is drawn.

Add a check that knows what the clip should show.

Two pieces of plumbing to verify first

Claude Code speaks Anthropic's Messages API format, so whatever sits in front of the model has to translate it. Ours lost the frames: each image either vanished or arrived as a block of text, and the model reviewed its work blind. Fixed in our test build, not yet on the hosted service. With any gateway, send one PNG first and check the model describes it.

Second, time. Our first call waited for the full answer instead of streaming it piece by piece. The worker, the process on the GPU machine that forwards requests to the server, gives up after 120 seconds, and the model was still thinking. Raising that to 30 minutes fixed the run, and the example now streams.

What fits on smaller cards

The 4-bit run peaked at 20.9 GiB. Smaller copies, one short request each:

Budget Copy Peak Result
16 GB 3-bit, 32K 13.7 GiB page renders, one dot visible at a time
12 GB 2-bit, 16K 10.0 GiB page cut off at 8,192 tokens

These ran on the 4090, not real 16 or 12 GB cards, with one sample each. The memory ladder, launch command and step-by-step setup for the Code2Video test have the rest. See also our earlier test of another SenseTime model, SenseNova-Loop-9B.

Credits and the honest limit

The SenseNova team at SenseTime built the model, the skill, the prompt template and the production runs, starting from the Qwen team's base model (model card, skill repository). bartowski made the GGUF quants and the llama.cpp maintainers made the server. Anthropic made Claude Code and Claude Opus 5.5, which drafted the brief from the authors' template. We first saw the model in an AI Search news video. We handled the deployment, fixed the image path, ran the sandboxed agent and counted the pixels.

This was one attempt at one brief under tight limits we chose. Logs, timings, the full VRAM table and the SDK example are in the complete Code2Video research post on inferencekey.com.

title: I built Diviso — a local-first AI agent that runs on your own machine, even on a phone
summary:
Most AI agents I tried wanted an account, a subscription, and my data on someone else's server. I wanted the opposite, so I built Diviso.

It's a Python agent that runs entirely on your own machine. Point it at a local model through Ollama, or plug in OpenAI, Claude, Grok, Gemini, Mistral, DeepSeek or OpenRouter with your own key. No Diviso account, no server of mine in the middle.

What's inside

  • ReAct loop + a planner, with hard step and cost caps on every run
  • Persistent memory (SQLite + a plain MEMORY.md) and TF-IDF search over your local files
  • A small multi-agent team (Researcher / Coder / Reviewer)
  • Tools for Python, JavaScript and Bash, file edits, tests, read-only git, web fetch — all behind an approval gate and a workspace sandbox
  • MCP client, a guarded scheduler, checkpoint/resume after every step
  • CLI + a small web dashboard

The part I'm happiest with

The core is standard-library-only Python, so the same code runs on a GPU PC, an old laptop, and an Android phone under Termux. It detects your hardware and picks a lite / balanced / pro profile with model sizes that actually fit.

Honest limits

It's v0.1.0. No token streaming yet, and the cloud providers are implemented against their documented APIs — the offline test suite (74 tests, CI green) runs on a deterministic mock provider. Local Ollama is the main path I test by hand.

Repo: https://github.com/Neuzant/diviso-agent

Feedback very welcome — especially from anyone who runs it on weird hardware.

title: The stock client is already post-quantum
summary:
I probed github.com's SSH service twice in one week, with the same tool and the same options. The first run, from my Ubuntu 24.04 laptop, said two post-quantum key exchanges worked only with the experimental Open Quantum Safe client. The second run, from a Debian 13 container, said the stock client and the experimental client negotiate identically.

GitHub had not changed anything. My client had. Debian 13 ships a newer OpenSSH, and that release already does what I was using an experimental build for.

This post is about that shift: stock OpenSSL and OpenSSH now negotiate post-quantum key exchange out of the box, which changes what a "stock versus experimental" comparison can tell you, and what a post-quantum audit should actually measure.

Part 4 of a series on building pqc-probe. Earlier: part 1, part 2, part 3.

What changed in the stock clients

Post-quantum key exchange arrived in the mainstream tools in a few releases:

Date Release Post-quantum key exchange
Apr 2025 OpenSSH 10.0 mlkem768x25519-sha256 becomes the default
8 Apr 2025 OpenSSL 3.5.0 default TLS key shares become X25519MLKEM768 and X25519
19 Sep 2024 OpenSSH 9.9 adds mlkem768x25519-sha256, enabled by default; adds the name sntrup761x25519-sha512
Apr 2022 OpenSSH 9.0 sntrup761x25519-sha512@openssh.com becomes the default

The OpenSSL change is easy to miss because it is one line in the source. The 3.5 default group list begins with ?*X25519MLKEM768, and the * means the client sends an ML-KEM hybrid key share in every handshake, next to a classical X25519 one. A server that understands ML-KEM can complete a post-quantum handshake without a single extra round trip. OpenSSL 3.0, still common on long-term-support distributions, has no ML-KEM at all.

OpenSSH went further in 10.1, which by default warns the user when a connection is not using a post-quantum key exchange.

Same server, two client machines

GitHub's SSH service offers three post-quantum key exchanges: mlkem768x25519-sha256, sntrup761x25519-sha512 and its older name sntrup761x25519-sha512@openssh.com. Here is what pqc-probe reported against it from each machine:

Ubuntu 24.04 laptop Debian 13 container
Stock SSH client OpenSSH 9.6p1 OpenSSH 10.0p2
mlkem768x25519-sha256 with the stock client not implemented completed
sntrup761x25519-sha512 with the stock client not implemented under this name completed
sntrup761x25519-sha512@openssh.com with the stock client completed completed
Stock versus OQS client diff 2 algorithms "only experimental" none

The laptop's OpenSSH 9.6 predates 9.9, so it lacks ML-KEM and the newer sntrup name. It still completes a post-quantum exchange through the older @openssh.com name, which every OpenSSH since 9.0 uses by default. The Debian container's 10.0 does all three.

The report from the laptop was correct; it described the laptop. Read naively, though, it suggested that GitHub needs an experimental client for ML-KEM, which is not true for anyone on a current OpenSSH.

What the diff still tells you

A "stock versus experimental" diff measures the gap between two clients against one server. When the stock client was classical-only, that gap was a fair stand-in for "what the server supports beyond the mainstream". With post-quantum stock clients, it splits into two different findings, and pqc-probe now labels them apart:

  • Newer mainline, not experimental. An algorithm only the OQS client negotiates may simply be one your stock client is too old for. pqc-probe marks these with the first mainline release that has them, for example mlkem768x25519-sha256 (stock OpenSSH since 9.9). The fix is to update the client, not to adopt an experimental build.
  • Genuinely experimental. Names such as frodokem-976-shake-sha384 or the @openquantumsafe.org hybrids exist only in OQS builds. A server that offers them is running experimental software, which is worth knowing for a different reason.

For TLS the effect is stronger. A stock OpenSSL 3.5 client already completes X25519MLKEM768 wherever the server allows it, so an empty TLS diff no longer means the server is classical. When the stock client itself negotiated a post-quantum group, pqc-probe says so in the report (vanilla_pq_capable), because the diff then says little about the server.

What it means for an audit

A connection is post-quantum only when both ends support it. A server audit answers half the question; the clients that actually connect answer the other half.

  1. Measure the server with a current client. Use OpenSSL 3.5+ and OpenSSH 10+ (or pqc-probe's Docker image, which carries both). An old client makes a capable server look incapable.
  2. Know your client population. Long-term-support systems keep their versions for years: Ubuntu 24.04 ships OpenSSH 9.6, which has sntrup761 but no ML-KEM, and OpenSSL 3.0, which has no post-quantum key exchange at all. Build agents, deploy scripts, backup jobs and the SSH clients on your own servers count too. Until they are upgraded, a server's ML-KEM support does nothing for their TLS connections, and their SSH connections stay on the older sntrup761 exchange.
  3. Record the client with the result. A finding such as "ML-KEM not negotiated" is meaningless without the client version that produced it. pqc-probe's JSON reports include the client versions for exactly this reason.

The practical consequence: "our servers support post-quantum key exchange" and "our connections are post-quantum" are two different claims, and only the second one protects traffic today against harvest-now, decrypt-later collection.

The comparison is shrinking, and that is good news

When I started pqc-probe, the interesting output was the diff: what the experimental client could do that the stock one could not. For the most common algorithms, that gap has largely closed. ML-KEM hybrids are in stock OpenSSL and OpenSSH, on by default, and negotiated without anyone asking for them.

That moves the useful question from "can it be done?" to "is it being done, by every client that matters?" The answer now depends far more on how old your clients are than on anything exotic on the server, and the cheapest post-quantum upgrade available to most teams is a routine package update.

Next in the series: shipping two liboqs builds in one container, and two GCC 14 bugs found on the way.

title: Introducing ONCSS: A Lightweight CSS-in-JS Library for Modern JavaScript Applications
summary:
I've been working on ONCSS, a CSS-in-JS library designed to make styling modern web applications simple, flexible, and developer-friendly.

Instead of writing separate CSS files for every component, ONCSS lets you define styles directly in JavaScript using a familiar object-based API.

Why ONCSS?

ONCSS provides a css() function that generates and injects CSS dynamically.

Here's a quick example:

import css from "oncss";

const button = css({
  backgroundColor: "#2563eb",
  color: "#fff",
  padding: "10px 20px",
  borderRadius: "8px",

  "&:hover": {
    backgroundColor: "#1d4ed8",
  },

  "@media (min-width: 768px)": {
    padding: "14px 28px",
  },
});

function Button() {
  return <button className={button}>Click mebutton>;
}

Features

  • Object-based CSS styling
  • Nested selectors and pseudo-classes
  • Responsive media queries
  • Custom breakpoints
  • Dynamic keyframes and animations
  • Global styles
  • CSS at-rules: @media, @container, @layer, @supports
  • Custom aliases and CSS property transformations
  • Configurable style injection
  • TypeScript support
  • Server-side rendering support

Installation 

npm install oncss

Built for flexibility

ONCSS also supports customization through configuration options such as classPrefix, breakpoints, aliases, injectStyle, and custom property handlers.

It also provides CSSFactory for collecting generated styles during server-side rendering.

I'm building ONCSS as an open-source project and would appreciate feedback from developers who work with React and modern JavaScript styling.

Check it out:

  • GitHub: https://github.com/devnax/oncss
  • npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/oncss

If you try it, I'd love to hear what you think and what features you'd like to see next.
